Overall, our results stand in contrast to the commonly held belief that, in nonconvex optimization, approximate computation of critical points is a tractable task.
item.dc:creator: Amir Ali Ahmadi, Georgina Hall

item.title: On the exact discretization of the $L_2$-norm in spaces generated by Rademacher functions and their $p$-adic analogues
item.description: arXiv:2608.25058v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sufficient conditions for the exact discretization of the $L_2$-norm in the space spanned by generalized Rademacher functions are proved. It is shown that the sufficient number of nodes for discretization with the minimal number of nodes is equal to $N$ or $N+1$ and depends on the dimension $N$. The conjecture of F.~Dai, A.~Prymak, V.~N.~Temlyakov, and S.~Yu.~Tikhonov on the positivity of weights in the exact discretization of the $L_2$-norm with a minimal number of points considered. It was investigated in which cases it holds and in which it fails for the spaces spanned by the $N$ generalized Rademacher functions with base $p$, and how the validity of the conjecture in this case depends on the parameters $p$ and $N$. The connection with generalized Hadamard matrices, the Hadamard's conjecture and Seberry's conjecture is demonstrated.
item.dc:creator: Anna Kazakova

item.title: Formulation-dependent linearized buckling of stiffened shell panels: role of the stress stiffness operator
item.description: arXiv:2609.22656v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Linearized buckling loads of stiffened panels can diverge across commercial shell formulations because six-degree-of-freedom elements treat drilling rotations and director kinematics differently in the stress stiffness operator. We derive three analytical stress stiffness operators (membrane-only, uncoupled rotational-block, and shear-coupled full second-variation forms), verified against an exact second-difference energy identity. Using direct matrix extraction in ANSYS (SHELL181, SHELL281) and modal and strain-energy benchmarks in Abaqus (S4, S8R), we classify these commercial elements across twelve configurations. On the finest cantilevered shear-panel mesh (in-plane bending and shear), the SHELL181 perturbation and classic procedures predict load factors 11.3% and 28.5% above an independent 3D continuum reference. By contrast, Abaqus S4 and ANSYS SHELL281 lie 5.2% and 5.8% below this reference and remain indistinguishable from the analytical full form within the junction-idealization uncertainty, while Abaqus S8R lies 20.1% below the reference. The tested cases indicate that substantial divergence occurs only when non-coplanar junctions carry pre-stress bending or transverse shear and the buckling mode involves junction drilling rotations. Under pure axial compression or uniform membrane shear flow, the analytical operators coincide and within-element procedures agree within 0.06%. Because buckling under in-plane bending and shear is formulation-dependent, stability design and layout optimization of built-up panels require cross-verification across shell elements or continuum models.
item.dc:creator: Lifeng Wang, Zhongli Qiu, Xuanhao Cheng, Run Du, Wenming Cheng, Min Xie, Xiong Rao

item.title: Superlinear Convergence of Cyclic Gradient Methods with Historical Ritz Step Sizes
item.description: arXiv:2610.32705v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The long-step Barzilai-Borwein (BB1) method, cyclic BB1, and limited memory steepest descent (LMSD) are special cases of limited memory steepest descent with retards (LMSDR), a family of methods using historical Ritz step sizes. We analyze a cyclic Ritz-step rule within LMSDR and a sampled LMSDR variant on strictly convex quadratics, seeking R-superlinear convergence guarantees in higher spectral dimensions. Let $n$ be the problem dimension and $m$ the history length. In exact arithmetic, we begin at $n=m+1$, the first dimension beyond the finite-termination case, and obtain an exact doubly exponential rate per gradient update for rolling reuse outside an explicit, possibly empty exceptional set. We extend this rate to nonempty open sets for $m+1<n\le2m$ when each Ritz step is reused $\ell\ge4$ times. To go beyond this range, we rebuild the history with $m$ sampling updates at each cycle. With positive sampling steps $\tau$ chosen in advance and factors $1-\tau\lambda_i$ uniformly bounded in modulus and away from zero, this gives almost-everywhere doubly exponential convergence when $(2\ell-1)^m>\binom{n-1}{m}$. For any $n>m$, increasing $\ell$ eventually satisfies this condition. Geometrically spaced choices among finitely many sampling lists preserve the guarantee.
item.dc:creator: Ran Gu

item.title: Certificate-Based Verification of Pulsed Field Ablation Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.18148v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Computational models of cardiac pulsed field ablation predict the lesion as the tissue where the electric field exceeds a lethal threshold. Their numerical error is rarely bounded, and automated pipelines increasingly run them without an expert checking each result. To verify each run, we separate the question "was the stated model solved correctly?" from the solver that answers it. An untrusted solver returns its answer with a certificate, which consists of a potential with the correct electrode and ground values and an exactly charge-conserving current. A small independent checker verifies the certificate against a written specification of the physics. Using the Prager-Synge hypercircle theorem evaluated in ball arithmetic, it turns the certificate into guaranteed two-sided bounds on the impedance and on the root-mean-square field of every tile of a lesion map, also over a range of blood/tissue conductivity ratios. The bounds cover numerical error only; whether the model describes tissue is a question of validation. A vectorized version of the checker takes about a tenth of our solver's time. For a focal electrode in contact, the tile-resolved depth at 1000 V and 700 V/cm is proven to lie in 3.50-3.75 mm for every ratio from 1.7 to 3.75. For a bipolar catheter, certified depths overlap published in-vivo depths. Where they differ from a published reference model, the certificates prove that the difference is not our numerical error. We compare the certificate with a grid convergence study on the same solver. On graded grids, the study is sharper for local fields but remains an estimate. On uniform grids, it fails to converge at the electrode edge, where the certificate still gives a valid bracket. Solvers that deliberately solve equations other than the specified ones pass the grid convergence study, but the certificates refute the impedances they report or leave them unsupported.
item.dc:creator: Konstantinos Dovelos

item.title: Fairness-optimized interlacing knots for even-degree periodic B-spline interpolation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30717v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interpolating an ordered set of points by a B-spline curve is a fundamental operation in computer-aided geometric design. Most of the literature addresses open curves, where the Schoenberg--Whitney condition characterizes a nonsingular collocation matrix and averaging is the standard way to choose the knot vector. Periodic B-spline interpolation has received much less attention, and the open-curve algorithms cannot be transferred directly. No theoretical criterion is available for choosing the knots, and the few existing constructions, such as the shifting and energy methods, remain empirical, with neither a theoretical guarantee nor a supporting analysis. This paper addresses this gap for even degrees. We prove that for every even degree $p\ge2$ the periodic collocation matrix is nonsingular whenever the domain knots and the interpolation parameters interlace, in either of two admissible orderings, for arbitrarily nonuniform parameters. Rather than singling out one knot vector, this sufficient condition delimits an $n$-parameter family of admissible knot vectors and provides the theoretical foundation for knot selection that periodic interpolation has lacked. It also explains why the empirical shifting method is solvable, previously justified only by an incorrect diagonal-dominance argument. We then exploit the remaining freedom to place the knots by fairness optimization, which preserves admissibility at every iterate and leads to the methods Opt-R and Opt-L. On four closed shapes with irregularly distributed points these methods achieve a fairness comparable to the shifting and energy methods, improve on them in several cases, and offer guarantees that no empirical construction provides.
